answer.rationale:
The single decision this cycle has to satisfy an 18% spend cut without adding delivery risk while the line runs at 94% of committed volume with no buffer. The tempting move is switch_primary_vendor, because memory_c2 says the low-cost vendor alone meets the mandate. That is exactly why memory_c2 is the one memory worth spending the verification budget on: it is the sole load-bearing claim behind the cheap-looking path, it is a consolidated summary rather than a source record, and its key qualifiers are unstated. 'Onboarding was quick and invoicing stayed accurate' is a cost-and-admin claim, not a delivery-reliability claim under a zero-buffer condition, and it does not say what volume, component criticality, or line utilization applied at the time. If that switch happened during a period with slack capacity or on a non-critical part, it does not transfer to a 14-day cutover on the primary contract with no buffer. A migration failure here is unrecoverable this cycle, whereas a pricing shortfall is revisitable at next review, so the asymmetry argues against the switch as the default.

I therefore intend negotiate_terms. memory_c4 says benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, and memory_c6 says longer commitments unlocked volume pricing without narrowing service scope; together these give two independent levers on total cost of ownership while memory_c1's stable integration is preserved and no migration work is introduced. Critically, the existence of a credible low-cost quote is itself the benchmark that makes the negotiation strong, so I capture most of memory_c2's value without absorbing its cutover risk. Scale is kept guarded: a shorter or staged term with a defined price floor, rather than locking a long multi-year commitment that would forfeit optionality if the incumbent underperforms or the low-cost vendor proves out later.

Remaining uncertainty is real and I am not resolving it: negotiation may close only part of the 18% gap, and I do not yet know whether the low-cost vendor can hold allocation at committed volume. memory_c3 (dual sourcing removed a single point of failure) points to add_second_source as the likely next-cycle move and the right way to qualify that vendor at low exposure rather than by betting primary supply on them. I am also flagging a downstream value risk: a hard percentage mandate creates pressure to treat unit price as the whole objective, which can quietly trade away quality, service scope, and supply resilience — costs that appear later as line stoppages rather than in this year's component line item. If the verified memory_c2 record shows the prior switch occurred at comparable volume, on a similarly critical component, and with buffer as thin as today's, I would upgrade switching to a serious contender and consider a staged cutover instead.
